title: The issue with 10x10 / German Volume Training
summary: NH dismantles 10x10 and German Volume Training. Volume means nothing without intensity, and 10x10 forces repeated sandbagging. Its 60-second rests make the cardiovascular system the limiter, and its large tonnage is low-quality. It is a short block borrowed from weightlifting that patches missing volume rather than a progressable rep scheme.
claims: Volume without intensity means nothing; it is only sets and reps until a load is applied
When people say volume they usually mean high reps, but 50 sets of 3 is high volume with low reps
High-volume training is equally low-intensity training; 10x10 lets you drop into low intensity windows when it does not have to
10x10 has the same sandbagging problem as 5x5 but worse: more sets and reps mean more sandbagging
In 10x10 you will hit sets limited by breathing and heart rate rather than muscular failure
There are two tonnages: total tonnage, including warm-ups, and relevant tonnage from hard sets; only the latter matters
Squatting 100 lb can accumulate tens of thousands of tonnage without growing your legs; it is cardio with a barbell
Three sets in a relevant intensity window could give better gains than 10x10
Prescribing 10x10 as a back-off set deep in a workout makes no sense
German Volume Training began with Olympic weightlifters, who use hypertrophy and strength blocks because they compete; bodybuilders do not need blocks
People swear by 10x10 because they never did volume before; jumping from sets of 5 to 10 doubles or quadruples tonnage and gives initial gains
True GVT is 10x10 with 60 seconds rest and a 4-0-2 tempo; nobody can do that with a real 70-75% of 1RM, so people use about 55-60%, which they could rep 20 times
The only static rep scheme without sandbagging is a single set; each added set moves you further from it
Prescriptions like 5x20 are bad for the same reasons
Within-session reps should decline when sets are real: 10, then 9 or 8; getting 10 on set two means you sandbagged set one
The goal of a session is to damage the muscle until it cannot return to a baseline relevant to absolute intensity, then rest so it grows
10x10 burns energy far beyond its results through cardiovascular and metabolic fatigue
High reps are good; repeating high-rep sets 10 times devalues them
10x10 simulates hardship: you feel breathless, sleep well and are sore, but that does not mean gains
A bodybuilding rep range you cannot repeat for a year with steady gains is not a good rep range
Pure tonnage-accumulation sets with no progression scheme should be at most 5% of training
Early 10x10 gains are cardiovascular and intra-workout recovery adaptations, not hypertrophy
10x10 progression is inflexible: adding one pound adds 100 lb of tonnage, so easy jumps mean the previous session was sandbagged
5x5 and 3x5 at least teach novices to do reps, regulate endurance and repeat form; 10x10 tends to break novices or become their religion
If a training method needs a big PED user as its poster boy, the method is probably bad
10x10 typically runs as a 4-6 week block, and NH advises against blocks; variation should live inside the program via rotations and evolving rep ranges
Needing a 10x10 block means volume was missing from your program; it is a band-aid on an axe wound
